page.text:
So far, our definitions have used `Describes: X`. That is, our
definitions do not specify a shape the entity being defined could have.

Mathlingua supports the following structures:

* `f(x_)` for mappings, i.e. entities that map and input to an output
* `(x, f(x_), (a, b)) for tuples, i.e. entities that are a fixed named
  sequence of items
* `{x_ : ...}` for collections, i.e. entities that are a collection of
  items

Note that `f(x_)` does not specify a *function* but instead only
something that associates inputs to outputs. For example `f(x)` maps `x`
to an output `f(x)` if `f` is a function, relation, etc. But also, `A(i,
j)` could be used to represent a matrix.

Similarly, `{x_ : ...}` doesn't necessarily mean a set but instead a
collection. That is, it could represent a set or a class.

That is consider the definition of a function:
```mlg
[\function:?on{A}:?to{B}]
Describes: f(x__) ::= y_
when: A, B is \set
specifies:
. x__ "in" A
. y_ "in" B
satisfies:
. forAll: x "in" A
  then:
  . existsUnique: y "in" B
    suchThat: f(x) = y
Documented:
. called: "function@[A]{ on $A?$}@[B]{ to $B?}$"
. written: "@[A, B]{f? \: : \: A? \rightarrow B?}"
Id: "1e0cb28d-bc8f-42db-bcfa-86a215e88c7a"
```

Notice that the definition describes that a `\function:on{A}:to{B}` has
the shape of mapping an input `x__` to the output `y_`. However, that
just describes the shape of the entity. The key characteristics of a
function is that it maps an input to a unique output, which is described
in the `satisfies:` section.

If the `Describes:` is of the form, `Describes: f(x_) ::= y_` then one
can write `f(x)`. That is, `f` must have exactly one input. If the
`Describes:` was instead `Describes: f(x_, y_) ::= z_` then one could
write `f(x, y)` but not `f(x)`. That is, the mapping is called with
exactly two arguments.

Here a symbol with a trailing `_` indicates a placeholder. This makes it
unambiguous to specify a mapping from a mapping's value. That is, `f(x_)`
represents a mapping `f` that takes one input, denoted `x_`. Note that
the name of the input doesn't matter. One could also write `f(t_)`.

On the other hand `f(x)` represents the value of `f` when applied to `x`.
Here the name `x` does matter, because `f(x)` only makes sense if the
symbol `x` is already defined.

Here, double trailing `_` indicates a *magnetic* placeholder. That is,
`f(x__)` means treat `f` as taking a single that is referenced as `x__`
but `f` can be written with multiple inputs that are converted to a
tuple.

An example will make this more clear. Consider `f(x__) ::= y_`. Then if
one writes `f(a, b)` then the call is treated like `f((a, b))`, i.e. a
single tuple input with `x__ := (a, b)`. For `f(a, b, c)` then the call
is treated like `f((a, b, c))`, i.e. `x__ := (a, b, c)`. Last, since a
tuple with one value is treated in Mathlingua as the value itself, `f(a)`
is treated like `f((a))` but `(a)` and `a` mean the same.

As a result, using `f(x__)` in the `Describes:` for our definition of a
function allows us to talk about a function as if it only has one input,
and still support multiple argument functions.

This way of describing multiple argument functions aligns with how multi
argument functions are classically specified in mathematical literature.
